instruction: Read only the public problem and document. Recover the distinct reasoning steps actually advocated, in your own concise ordinary English. A step links a stated or clearly implied reason to a concrete mechanism/action and its intended consequence. Keep roles, ordering, conditions and scope. Do not fill in unstated reasoning. Separate distinct causal applications, merge duplicates, and abstain on unsupported or unresolved ones. Return any number of steps. For each give premise, action, consequence, and quote (one exact contiguous source passage supporting the step). Use [] if none. No fixed vocabulary or reference answers are supplied.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A whole district is difficult to hold in mind on a short walk. Build the route around how the neighborhood uses the river and let each stop reveal a different answer in a resident's voice.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: Visitors arriving by bus need a starting point they can recognize before pressing play. Begin beside a permanent feature visible from the stop and include a close photograph of it on the tour page.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A route that ends near its beginning makes the return trip easier to judge. Walk a compact loop and time it with generous pauses for looking and listening before advertising its duration.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: The river can be busy enough to drown out the best line in an interview. Test listening positions at the time visitors are likely to walk and move a stop inland if its speech disappears.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A visitor following an interview may walk right past the building it describes. Open each stop with one precise visual cue and ask listeners to settle there before the story begins.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: Intersections demand a person's full attention. End the track on the near pavement and let the next one start across the street so visitors can cross at their own pace with the audio paused.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A row of nearly identical warehouses invites wrong turns. Photograph the distinctive end wall from the direction of travel and reuse that viewpoint on the map where the turn occurs.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: The shortest path on a preview map may involve steps by the water. Walk the level alternative, describe its surfaces and add its rejoining point so listeners can choose a route before setting out.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A resident's memory lands differently when listeners can inspect something it mentions. Ask interviewees to bring the interviewer to a surviving detail, then record what they notice while standing beside it.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: An interview may include a family story its speaker later wants to keep private. Play the edited extract to the speaker and agree on its wording, credit and public use before including it.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: Two neighbors may remember the same landing differently. Let each locate the memory in time and speak in their own voice so listeners can hear how the place changed between their accounts.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A historical date in a script sounds authoritative even when it came from a guess. Check dates against a named local record and place the source beside the transcript for readers who want to follow it.

documents.text: Spoken directions can sound obvious at a desk and fail within seconds on the street. Give an early cut to a newcomer, walk a few paces behind and note where they have to look back.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: One long recording forces walkers to match an editor's pace. Publish a separate short track for each stop so a listener can linger over a mural or skip ahead after a detour.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A stairwell or underpass may interrupt a mobile connection. Offer the recordings and map as a download at the start so a listener can take the whole walk offline.

documents.text: A listener who uses captions may miss the significance of a sound between lines of speech. In the transcript, identify the ferry bell or tools when that sound carries part of the story.

documents.text: An abrupt jump from a quiet narrator to a busy workshop can make people pull off their headphones. Compare track levels on ordinary earbuds and soften transitions while retaining the character of the setting.

documents.text: A long street name can be hard to recognize when heard only once. Pair stop titles with the same plain place names on the map, player and direction signs that a visitor will consult.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: A visitor who needs a rest should be able to judge how far remains. Mark verified benches and the distance to the next stop on the map, including stretches with nowhere to sit.

documents.text: Listeners gather where a recording tells them to stand. Choose listening spots back from doorways and narrow walkways, then test whether a small group can stop there while others pass.

documents.text: When a path closes temporarily, a printed arrow can send people to a locked gate. Keep a dated route notice on the tour page with an alternate approach to the affected stop.

documents.problem: A volunteer arts group wants to make a short audio walking tour of its riverside neighborhood. How could it turn local voices and places into a walk that visitors can find, follow and enjoy on their own?
documents.text: Not everyone wants to install an app for a half-hour walk. Give the tour a short, readable web address on the starting notice so someone can type it or share it aloud.

documents.text: A listener who knows the area may spot a mistaken name months after launch. Put a correction contact beside each transcript and ask for the stop title so volunteers can locate the disputed passage.

documents.text: A loop can end by returning the listener to a sound they heard differently at the start. Revisit the river at the final stop and leave a brief silence for the real waterfront to answer.
